abstract_preview: The increasingly complex energy systems are turning the attention towards model-free control approaches such as reinforcement learning (RL). This work proposes novel RL-based energy management approaches for scheduling the operation of controllable devices within an electric network. The proposed approaches provide a tool for efficiently solving multi-dimensional, multi-objective and partially observable power system problems. The novelty in this work is threefold: We implement a hierarchical RL-based control strategy to solve a typical energy scheduling problem. Second, multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is put forward to efficiently coordinate different units with no communication burden. Third, a control strategy that merges hierarchical RL and MARL theory is proposed for a robust control framework that can handle complex power system problems. A comparative performance evaluation of various RL-based and model-based control approaches is also presented. Experimental results of three typical energy dispatch scenarios show the effectiveness of the proposed control framework. ## 1. Introduction The evolution towards decarbonized energy systems is entailing deep changes at the levels of generation and demand. From one side, the integration of more renewable energy sources is bringing stochastic ity and random fluctuations to the generation side. At the load side, the emergence of prosumers and the movement towards the electrification of transport and heating are increasing the uncertainty and peaks on the demand side. The power flow is becoming bi-directional with an increasing number of distributed energy resources (DERs), thereby fostering a decentralized grid architecture with multiple decision-making units. The integration of an efficient energy management system (EMS) for optimizing the increasingly complex power-flow streams is there fore paramount. The traditional way for operating an energy system supposes perfect system dynamics’ knowledge, complete understand ing of the generation–demand behavior and full controllability over generation sources, which is no longer valid under the realm of high uncertainties and decentralization. Considering the rapidly improving control algorithms and computational capabilities, more sophisticated and up-to-the-minute control approaches are needed for coping with the challenges of future electric grids and staying in line with the rapid changes. EMSs can be categorized into centralized, decentralized and dis tributed approaches [1,2]. Centralized EMSs require a central unit that oversees the dispatchable resources and control them accordingly. Such a framework usually raises scalability, communication burden and cybersecurity problems. In decentralized approaches, each dispatchable unit has its own controller with no need for exchanging information among units. Although flexible, such approaches lack an overall coordination level as each controller aims to optimize its own utility function. In distributed approaches, dispatchable resources exchange information in real time in order to achieve an optimal management. However, distributed control is usually difficult to implement and its real-time communication requirements usually increase as the number of controlled units increases. In the context of decentralized and distributed energy management strategies, the application of multi-agent systems has been receiving an increasing level of attention in the area of power system energy management. A multi-agent system can be defined as a framework composed of a set of interacting and autonomous units that take actions independently. This interest is motivated by the fact that the emerging electric networks feature a distributed architecture, which require an optimal coordination between different homogeneous and heterogeneous interconnected decision-making units (e.g., DERs, residential loads, electric vehicle (EV) chargers, etc.) linked by market transactions and physical electric flows with the overall objectives of reaching a sustainable, cost-effective, stable and reliable operation of a given network [3]. Environments where decentralized and distributed control approaches could emerge are eco-neighborhoods and microgrids (gridconnected or islanded) composed of a set of loads, renewable generation, energy storage systems (ESSs), capacitor banks, etc. Typical objectives here would be to find the optimal dispatch of controllable resources in order to meet the load with the minimum environmental impact, and maximum benefits for suppliers and customers. Other ob jectives of interest include peak shaving, power fluctuations reduction, maintaining customer comfort, voltage regulation, etc. Multi-agent modeling of energy management problems is therefore becoming more evident to account for this diversity in objectives, and, primordially, the distributed nature of decision-making entailed by DER installations. Various studies have proposed multi-agent frameworks for solving typical energy management problems of power systems as have been highlighted in various studies such as [4–6]. The most common computational approaches that are typically incorporated within EMSs are essentially rule-based or model-based (e.g. dynamic programming, stochastic programming, model predictive control (MPC), heuristic ap proaches). In general, a model-based approach requires a precise model of the underlying system dynamics, a predictor for forecasting the sources of uncertainty, and a solver for solving the problem in real time operations. The main limitation of a model-based approach is its reliance on a precise system model; this is not realistic in practice, especially in highly uncertain environments where obtaining an accurate model is usually difficult and costly. Its performance is also dependent on the predictions’ quality of the uncertainty sources (gen eration, demand, electricity prices, etc.) [7]. Furthermore, model-based approaches lack adaptability and may not be computationally efficient for real-time control, as many approaches require the reiteration of al the computations whenever a new decision is to be taken. For optimization problems in particular, besides their reliance on models and predictions, tractability issues could emerge with increased numbers of decision-making units, especially if the corresponding optimization problem formulations require integer variables—like energy storage. Optimization-based approaches require as well the re-iteration of com putations whenever a decision is to be made. This may be challenging h l l d b f d d d h bl relatively small intervals of time. To overcome these limitations, model-free and data-driven approaches have been proposed in the literature. As have been reviewed in many studies such as [3,8–13], there is an increasing interest towards the application of reinforcement learning (RL), a data-driven decision making approach, in solving typical energy management problems. In general, RL is a branch of machine learning (ML) in which an agent acquires the ability of solving one or many given tasks through interaction with its surrounding environment. To learn solving a task, the agent takes actions and subsequently receives rewards from the environment, which reflects how good its action was. Based on the collected experience, the agent progressively learns how to take actions in the direction that maximizes the rewards obtained. The growing attention surrounding RL is motivated by the success it has achieved mainly in the fields of robotics and games as it was able to reach superhuman intelligence in complex video games such as Atari, the game of go, and others [14]. Such features make RL algorithms potential candidates for solving complex control problems in the area of power systems. Inspired by the success achieved by RL in various fields, it could be, by analogy, a potential enabler of the smart grid vision when adequately integrated in power system decision and control problems. The ability of RL algorithms to efficiently solve complex problems makes them potential candidates for solving sophisticated control and decision-making problems in the area of energy management. That is, RL can enable the automation of grid operation while flexibly handling the increased complexity and uncertainty in energy systems. Indeed, it can provide a strategic tool that ensures a robust, adaptive, tactical, fast and anticipative decision making, which perfectly fits the requirements of the rapidly changing energy landscape. Compared with model-based approaches, the reliance on deep learning can help accelerate the integration of DERs by reducing upfront control design time and costs as new resources are put online. Nevertheless, the use of model-free RL does not have to be disruptive to existing modeling efforts, but it rather tends to play a complementary role in order to reach higher levels of adaptability and flexibility. In contrast to optimization-based approaches, RL involves agents that can generate decisions instantaneously by performing a simple policy-evaluation step. This characteristic makes deep RL a perfect fit for applications involving real-time decision making. When applied to other domains, RL has proven to be a viable mean for optimally orchestrating the operation of different system resources while taking into account their specific traits and uncertainties. Bringing the expertise of RL to the area of power system decision and control can potentially provide a flexible tool that overcomes the limitations of traditional (rule-based and model-based) control approaches and ensures a fast and efficient decision making in highly complex and uncertain environments. These motivations clearly justify the increasing interest towards the application of RL as a data-driven decision making tool for solving typical power system decision and control problems. Although the research on the application of RL in the area of energy management is advancing constantly, the present approaches are focus ing on single-agent reinforcement learning (SARL)-based control strate gies which limits the applicability of RL to specific small-scale scenarios, while the emerging electric and energy networks are becoming increasingly multi-dimensional [3]. The application of SARL approaches for solving problems that require complex coordination among agents usually yields poor performance, and may result in a curse of dimensionality when the number of actions is relatively large [15,16]. In this regard, multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) is a promising active research field that joins the merits of both multi-agent systems and data-driven approaches, and can efficiently handle decision-making problem in a multi-agent environment featuring uncertainties and com plexities. In this work, we provide a novel vision for operating the grid of the future through proposing a control framework that can deal with complex and uncertain power and energy systems with the overall objective of promoting autonomous, sustainable and costeffective operation. More specifically, we seek to design, implement and compare efficient and robust MARL-based control strategies in the area of energy management within microgrids and eco-neighborhood. Here, an eco-neighborhood is understood to be a self-productive community of multi-dwelling residential buildings endowed with various DERs to reduce its common reliance on conventional generation with high greenhouse gas emissions. The rest of this work is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews related work and highlights the main contributions of our proposed control framework. Sections 3 and 4 describe and formulate the stud ied control problems. The proposed RL-based control strategies are described in Section 5 along with an introduction to hierarchical RL. Experimental results are reported in Section 6 with a discussion about the results and their applicability. Finally, the paper is concluded in Section 7. ## 2. Related work ## 2.1. MARL approaches in power & energy systems The application of MARL for solving typical energy management problems in the area of power systems is receiving an increasing attention. MARL is a promising field that can model each decisionmaking unit as an autonomous agent that takes actions based on its local observation [17]. Although promising, the application of MARL in power system decision and control is still in its early stages as only a few works in this field have been proposed recently in the literature [3,10]. In particular, a multi-agent control scheme has been developed in [18] to enable energy sharing between buildings with the overall aim of reaching a zero-energy community status. Each building, modeled by an agent, learns its control strategy independentl based on deep Q-learning (DQL), and learns to cooperate with its neighbor buildings through shared rewards. Ref. [19] combines a mult Q-learning based algorithm with an artificial neural network for solving a typical DR-based energy management problem in a residential house. In [20], a fully decentralized multi-agent scheme for reducing the electricity bill and user dissatisfaction through the optimal hour-ahead scheduling of home appliances and an EV load has been presented. In an energy market framework, [21] presented an energy and load management strategy based on a distributed MARL approach. Although these studies (i.e., [18–21]) have highlighted many of the advantages offered by MARL when applied to energy management frameworks, their main limitation is that they are based on Q-learning and its h hl h d h bl f h h h they can solve problems only with discrete action spaces. In the case of controllable units with continuous action spaces such as ESS or heating ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) units, a discretization of the action space is required which, in turn, can result in sub-optimal solu tions. Therefore, it would be of interest to investigate approaches that allow the use of continuous action spaces (e.g., approaches that rely on the principle of deep deterministic policy gradient (DDPG), which, so far, have rarely been applied in energy management problems. Another limitation of these approaches is that they are based on the category o independent learning. This is the simplest, as it is based on the naive extension of single-agent approaches. Particularly, in those each agen learns independently and treats other agents as part of its environment Although simple, independent learning-based approaches are compu tationally expensive and do not perform well in environments where elaborate coordination between agents is required. Furthermore, their control environments fall victim to non-stationarity because agents policies are updated simultaneously. and policies change from the perspective of each individual agent. It is noted that environmen stationarity is a crucial assumption necessary for the convergence of RLbased algorithms. In multi-agent environments, ensuring a stationary environment is possible only if each agent has knowledge about other agents’ policies; this is challenging in practice, as agents are usually required to act independently based on their local observations only. In addition, independent learning may not yield acceptable results in applications that involve complex coordination among agents [15,16, 22,23]. To overcome the control environment’s non-stationarity issue, [24, 25] have proposed to solve energy management problems based on centralized training decentralized execution. That is, during the training phase, each agent learns a control policy using feedback signals from a centralized critic network that has access to common information about all agents. In contrast, the execution phase is fully decentralized in the sense that each agent only needs its local observation for gen erating a decision [15,16,22]. The work presented in [24] solves an energy management problem within an industrial microgrid with high renewable generation by a multi-agent proximal policy optimization (PPO) approach. The objective is to coordinate the different machines to reduce current and predicted overall energy cost. The authors in [25] have solved a typical demand side management problem under real time pricing by multi-agent PPO through modeling each household as an agent. These energy management approaches, which are founded on PPO, are known to handle problems with both continuous and/or discrete action spaces. These proposed approaches are based on primitive RL with one-layer control policy that generates a decision in a single time step. This is contrary to skills or temporally-abstracted actions as in other RL categories. As energy management problems are becoming increasingly complex, primitive RL may not be adequate to learn sufficiently complex strategic actions. Furthermore, some real control problems may violate the Markov property that supposes, given information at the present time, the future of the given process is independent of its past. Furthermore, a fundamental Markovian property is the stationarity of the environment transition dynamics and rewards. Such assumptions are basic for the development of RL algorithms, and is therefore required for their proper functioning and convergence to an optimal solution. For illustration, if we consider the context of a demand response program, the decisions of an RL based controller are influenced by the knowledge of the history of energy consumption and electricity prices, which clearly violates the Markovian property. Another illustration is that of an RL agent that is controlling DERs within a power system with deep penetration of renewables. On one hand, the RL controller needs to flexibly adapt to the rapidly changing and stochastic variations of renewables and load. On the other, the weather dependency of these resources is making the control environment non-stationary, which poses a challenge. Therefore, approaches that can overcome the underlying non-Markovian dependencies in energy management problems need to be put forward. Another point that has not been taken into account in existing multi agent based energy management frameworks is that there is a risk of overfitting to the control policies of other agents. Such problem is more likely to occur when each agent learns a deterministic onelayer control policy rather than a stochastic policy, a hierarchy or an ensemble of policies during the training phase. In this case, the agents may not perform well during the execution phase when one of the agents changes its control strategy. Therefore, there is a need for developing a control framework that is robust to changes in the control policies of different agents. However, no solutions have been provided in the literature to address all these issues in multi-agent frameworks. Although RL is a wide research area with diverse sub-areas, the choice of RL algorithms in the area of power systems is focusing on a very limited choice of simple algorithms, while a large part of RL’s potential is still unexplored. In their thorough studies, [3,12,26] have highlighted the need for applying new and diverse RL-based approaches to solve various case studies of typical energy management problems. In this direction, hierarchical RL, a promising sub-area of RL, appears to be a potential alternative in this regard. Hierarchical RL intends to solve complicated problems by decomposing them through learning spatiotemporal abstract actions rather than primitive actions. Moreover, it can cope better with non-Markovian dependencies. Further, merging hierarchical RL with MARL theory can potentially give rise to highly performing and highly robust control strategies where different agents are coordinated and set to jointly learn spatio-temporally extended ac tions in much more complex and uncertain environments. For instance, the control hierarchy for generating actions is not composed of only one layer—as in primitive RL—, but rather it is extended to multi-layers in the space and/or time dimensions. Another research gap is the lack of benchmarking through the provision of comparative evaluations of diverse RL algorithms when solving the same energy management tasks [27]. Furthermore, there are no studies that provide a thorough comparison between RL-based energy management approaches and other common approaches such as MPC, which is known to cope well with environment uncertainties. Such comparisons are required to investigate the merit of RL and highlight the trade-offs of each approach. ## 2.2. Contributions The main contributions of this work are: • <sub>We map typical energy management problems in the area of mi-</sub> crogrid and eco-neighborhood energy dispatch as Markov games. These mappings consider load and generation uncertainty as well as the environment partial observability. • <sub>We propose and compare various model-free MARL-based control</sub> strategies that can flexibly address the aforementioned gaps in a unified framework. In particular, our proposed control framework can flexibly cope with the challenging multi-objective energy management problems featuring high dimensional state and action spaces. Unlike the classical approaches, like MPC, which require significant investment in upfront engineering resources needed to build and maintain an explicit model and forecasting of the power and energy system, our proposed approaches do not require any predictions or system modeling and are adaptable to the control environment changes and its underlying uncertainties because of deep-RL’s learning feature. To overcome the limitations of centralized approaches and real-time communication burden, all our proposed control strategies are based on the principle of centralized training decentralized execution (CTDE). In fact, during the learning phase which is offline and centralized, each dispatchable unit learns to coordinate with other units through the sharing of information to reach desired ob jectives. On the other hand, real-time control execution is fully decentralized where each unit takes actions based on its local observations with no need for any communication with neighboring units or a central coordinating controller. Further, our proposed control schemes can solve control problems involving dispatchable units with continuous and/or discrete action space, and is applicable to fully cooperative, fully competitive or mixed cooperative-competitive problems. • <sub>We demonstrate, for the first time, the potential of hierarchical</sub> RL for both single-agent and multi-agent problems in the area of power systems. Such choice is motivated by the potential of hierarchical RL in terms of generating high-performance and robust control policies. A novel approach at the intersection of hierarchical RL and MARL is proposed in order to give rise to performant and robust control strategy in the area of power systems control. The scalability of the proposed multi-agent hierarchical RL-based control approach within a microgrid is investigated to prove that it can handle control problems with high-dimensional action space. Furthermore, to evaluate its potential in handling uncertainties, we contribute a comparison between the multiagent hierarchical RL-based solution and commonly accepted receding horizon MPC-based solution. • <sub>To validate the performance of the proposed control approaches</sub> and promote their applicability, we study three typical energy management problems within microgrid and eco-neighborhood based on realistic data. A comparison between the various proposed RL-based approaches is also presented for benchmarking purposes. ## 3. Control problem description In general, we consider a system composed of various intercon nected electrical components including non-controllable loads and DERs, as shown in Fig. 1. These DERs can be small-scale generators such as diesel generator, controllable loads (e.g. HVAC, EV, etc.), ESSs, etc. The system can be self-sufficient relying on its internal resources for meeting the demand or can receive backup from a stiff source (e.g. electricity provider, main grid, etc.). Overall, the main objective within such system is to optimally manage the electric flows through an optimal dispatch of controllable units in order to meet the load with an optimal operation cost and reduced negative environmental impact. Such control framework is inherently multi-objective with high-dimensional state and action spaces as it features a set of interconnected and interacting units linked by electrical flows and market transactions. For the sake of illustration and without loss of generality, we con sider solving three power system optimal decision and control problems that are typical instantiations of the previously described system: ![](86a69a9554cd344faf4802f153609d5ca123385a87cf5845735a2d011ebe9908.jpg) Fig. 1. Control environment. • <sub>Problem (A): A microgrid in islanded mode with residential load,</sub> one ESS, a diesel generator and high PV production. The objective is to implement an energy dispatch strategy for determining the optimal charging/discharging power for the ESS in order to meet the load, maximize self-consumption from PV generation, and minimize diesel generator operation cost. • <sub>Problem (B): An eco-neighborhood consisting of two multi-</sub> dwelling residential buildings, two ESSs and a shared PV production. The objective is to find the optimal coordination among the ESSs in order to reduce the energy purchased from the electricity provider while reducing power fluctuations and peaks of the aggregated demand power profile, which is beneficial for the electricity provider. • <sub>Problem (C): An islanded microgrid with a diesel generator, four</sub> distributed behind-the-meter ESSs and high PV production. The objective is to optimally coordinate the ESSs with the diesel generator to meet the load while optimizing the operation cost and maximizing self-consumption from renewable generation. The three problems are fully cooperative since the units under control have a common goal to achieve. Further, the problems are multi-objective and featuring uncertainties (from load and PV), and they have high-dimensional state spaces. Another challenge is that the control environments are partially observable because a noisy observation is usually obtained instead of a state, while the load and renewable production cannot be exactly known in advance at the beginning of each time step. To handle the underlying complexities and uncertainties, the proposed problems are first formulated, and then solved by hierarchical RL and MARL-based strategies. It is noted that Problem (A) is a single agent decision-making problem, as it requires the optimal dispatch of only one ESS. The objective of considering such problem here is explained in detail in the subsequent sections; it will be used to highlight the merit of hierarchical RL in comparison to primitive RL. Problems (B) and (C) involve two or more decision-making units, and are therefore regarded as multi-agent problems. ## 4. Control problems To formulate an energy management problem as a Markov game, each dispatchable unit is represented as a separate agent that can take control actions based on its local observations. Then, depending on the system and its components, the observation space, action space and reward function of each agent are defined. The observation space at a given time step designates local informa tion that is accessible to an agent prior to taking an action. Taking the example of a group of ESS wherein each ESS is modeled as an agent, the local observation available to a particular ESS can be its state of charge (SOC). Unless a communication network is available, a given ESS does not have knowledge about the SOC of other ESS within the same group. We consider another example of an HVAC system that is responsible for controlling set-point temperatures within a building with multiple zones. If each zone is modeled as an agent. its local observation can include a measurement of its current ambient temperature, but not those of its neighboring zones. The global state space is usually the assembly of local observa tions of all agents combined with any other information about the overall system’s state. If we consider the same example of coordi nating a group of ESS, the global state embraces SOCs of all agents. Other useful information that could be incorporated within the global state include the aggregated demand and generation (dispatchable and non-dispatchable) at the current time step. The action space reflects the admissible range or set of actions that can be taken by an agent at a given time step. Therefore, the action space can be continuous or discrete. It is said to be continuous when the action can take any value from within an interval. In case an agent selects actions from a finite set, the action space is referred to as discrete space. By way of illustration, a HVAC unit modeled as an agent can have a discrete action space if the action involves a decision about its ON/OFF status. It can also have a continuous action space if its set-point temperature need to be regulated at a given time step. In this case, the action space is the interval ranging from minimum to maximum admissible indoor temperature. If we take the example of a diesel generator that is modeled as an agent, its action space is simply the interval ranging from its minimum to maximum power output. Lastly, the reward assigned to a specific agent designates its desired goal and can reflect either an incentive or a penalty. For instance, if the aim is to make specific agents learn how to minimize the operation cost issuing from conventional generation, the reward penalizes any power drawn from fossil-fuel based generators. Alternatively, if the objective within a microgrid is to maximize the power sold to the main grid, a reward is allocated to agents for any surplus of production bought by the main grid. Based on the description above, the elements of a Markov game model of each control problem vary depending on the various com ponents that constitute the control environment. For the sake of illus tration, details are provided about the formulation of problems (A), (B) and (C) as Markov games. ## 4.2.1. Problem (A) In this problem, the objective is to find the optimal charging/discharging power for the ESS, which is modeled as a separate agent. We choose the local observation of the ESS agent to be composed of its current SOC and the history of load consumption and PV production in the previous � time steps (here � is a hyperparameter). It is noted that the use of a history of observations is a common way for dealing with partial observability. The action space of the ESS agent is the range between its maximum discharging and charging powers. The diesel generation here serves as a back-up generator that compensates at best for any lack or surplus of capacity and energy by following net load variations. It is assumed that the diesel generator has a maximum power output that cannot be exceeded. In case the combined action of all generation sources (i.e., diesel power output added to renewable generation and ESS discharging) is insufficient for supplying the demand, load shedding is performed and results in unserved load. In the case of a generation surplus occurs due to high PV generation, low demand and fully charged ESS, the excess is simply curtailed. A penalty is associated to the agent for any unserved load or if the diesel generator has been employed. Our Markov game formulation suggests that the information that each ESS needs for real-time execution is only its SOC and the history of aggregated load and renewable generation. Therefore, a given ESS does not share any information about its current energy state with other DERs. and only needs to receive information about the history of aggregated demand and generation which are made available through a simple one-point measurement (e.g. at the point of common coupling) or through local state estimation [29]. The use of aggregated profiles rather than individual ones is a way for alleviating privacy concerns as each ESS agent does not reveal any details about its individual state in real time especially when privately-owned behind-the-meter ESSs are involved. Furthermore, agents do not need to communicate their current state to any entity. Such a scheme is also realistic in the sense that a system operator does not need to collect measurements from multiple, different points in the microgrid (especially from behind-themeter DERs) which entails a high communication and sensing burden besides to raising concerns over customer privacy [30]. Proposed control approaches Once the problem is formulated as a Markov Game as detailed in the previous section, specific control algorithms are then implemented to solve specific problems. Here, the proposed MARL approaches are offline-learning and CTDE-based. In this section, the principle of CTDE is first introduced and its advantages are presented. Proposed control strategies for solving problems are then described. ## 5.1. Principle of centralized-training decentralized execution Prior to describing the principle of CTDE, two elemental compo nents of any RL algorithm are defined, namely the Q-function and V-function. The Q-function quantifies the value of taking action � under state � at time � while following control policy �, and is defined as follows [10]: $$ Q ^ {\pi} (s, a) = \mathbb {E} [ \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {T} \gamma^ {k} r _ {t + k} | S _ {t} = s, a _ {t} = a ]\tag{4} $$ The V-function represents the value of a state � when following a policy � [10]: $$ V ^ {\pi} (s) = \mathbb {E} [ \sum_ {k = 0} ^ {T} \gamma^ {k} r _ {t + k} | S _ {0} = s ]\tag{5} $$ CTDE, a common category in MARL, features various advantages when solving multi-agent problems. As any RL algorithm, it comprises a training phase in which agents are trained to generate optimal actions, and an execution phase in which each agent uses its learned control policy for taking decisions in real time. As the name suggests, the training phase in CTDE is centralized in the sense that it uses a central unit, called the critic network, that has access to information of all agents $( \mathrm { i . e . , }$ local observations, actions and rewards) and guides the learning process of the agents. The use of such common information during the training phase is an implicit way for sharing information among agents; therefore, it can address the non-stationarity issue and promote a better coordination among the agents. In this work, our focus is on actor–critic based CTDE approaches, where each agent learns two deep neural networks during the training phase: • <sub>The actor network is a parameterized representation of the control</sub> policy �. It is trained based on the feedback provided by a critic network in order to provide better control actions. The actor network receives a local observation as input, and outputs optimal actions. • <sub>The critic network is a parameterized representation of a Q or V-</sub> function which quantifies the value of an action. It is trained to learn how to generate better evaluations of the actions taken in a given state. The critic network takes the global state (i.e., a grouping of all agents’ observations) and global actions (i.e., a grouping of all agents’ actions), and outputs a scalar value that judges the obtained actions (i.e., whether it is a good action or not). For the sake of illustration, as we consider ESS agents in this study, Fig. 2 illustrates the inputs and outputs of the actor and critic networks of each ESS agent (based on the description provided in the previous section). Fig. 3 illustrates the training and execution phases of an actor–critic based CTDE approach where the critic network is the parameterized representation of the Q-function. In multi-agent settings, each agent usually has its own actor and critic network. Through the training process, each agent regularly updates its actor and critic networks by adjusting their weights. These updates are based on a set of data sequence or random data samples from an experience replay buffer that stores the history of interaction of the agents with the environment (i.e. observations, actions and obtained rewards). Commonly, the critic network update is based on Temporal Difference (TD) while the actor network update is Policy-Gradient (PG) based. At the end of the training phase, each agent has learned to generate optimal actions, and will use its learned control policy during the execution phase for taking real-time decisions. In the execution phase, the centralized critic networks are no longer needed, and each agent uses only its own actor network to generate actions based on its local observations. Therefore, the execution phase is said to be decentralized because each agent only uses its local real-time information for generating actions with no need for communication or sharing information with other agents or a central coordinator. ![](481ae98b6c265f20f43920d27a554a32d795cd218eb75f489d87243534814850.jpg) Fig. 3. Actor and critic networks of one agent during training and execution phases. Such framework is suitable for power system applications, because the emerging systems are becoming increasingly multi-dimensional and decentralized. In this case, CTDE allows to reliably solve problems in volving various interconnected decision-making units while accommodating sensing, communication and privacy issues. In CTDE, each agent acts autonomously (without the need for any external dispatch signal) based on its local observations. In general, CTDE-based approaches join the merits of both centralized and decentralized approaches. It is known that the main limitation of a purely decentralized approach is that it is difficult to reach a higher coordination level among the controllable resources. CTDE overcomes this issue through its centralized training phase where agents learn to cooperate and coordinate their actions for reaching the desired objectives. By the end of the training phase, each agent has acquired the skill of achieving the required tasks while collaborating with the other agent. The learned skills allow each agent to take appropriate decisions even when operating in a decentralized way. Autonomous decision making and no reliance on real-time exchange of information within CTDE can be seen as an advantage over centralized approaches. Furthermore, any issue that may disturb the operation of one agent, does not, at all, affect the other ESS operation, which results in a highly reliable operation. The characteristic of decentralized execution is also of interest in applications requiring enhanced levels of privacy where real-time exchange of information is a major concern (e.g., in demand response). CTDE allows each agent to take actions based on its local observations only with no need for exchanging its state with neighboring units nor receiving their local state. ## 5.2. Multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient The multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (MADDPG) method, proposed in [28]. is an adaptation of the classical actor-critic method to deal with a multi-agent setting, and is based on CTDE. In multi agent frameworks, classical Q-learning and PG approaches face the challenge of non-stationarity and high variance, respectively. MADDPG has proven to effectively overcome these challenges, and performs well in multi-agent settings with continuous and/or discrete action spaces [28]. With MADDPG, an actor and critic network must be obtained for each agent during the training phase. In general, an actor model receives an observation and generates an action. The critic model, as its name suggests, receives the action and state as input, and generates a value that represents an evaluation of the action (whether it is a good action or not based on the generated reward). To deal with the non-stationarity in multi-agent settings, each critic network is augmented with the states and actions of all other agents. However, each actor only needs its local observation as input for making decisions. During the training phase, the critic, which has more input information about the agents, acts as a guide for its corresponding actor to make it learn how to choose better actions, while the critic learns how to generate better judgments. The actor and critic networks are updated based on PG and TD-learning, respectively. It is noted that the critic networks are only needed during the training phase. During the execution phase (validation and testing), only the actor networks—which need local information only—are used to make decisions [28]. Hierarchical reinforcement learning control strategies ## 5.4.1. Hierarchical reinforcement learning As we deal with power system problems of increasing complexity at many levels, the use of primitive RL-based approaches may not be sufficient to learn efficient control strategies. The application of hierarchical $R L , { \textbf { a } }$ sub-area of RL, can be a potential alternative to primitive RL because it intends to solve complicated problems by learning spatio-temporal abstract actions rather than primitive ones. The control architecture of primitive RL is composed of only one control layer, while in hierarchical RL, the control hierarchy is multi-layer, and these layers can be extended in space and/or time dimensions. The concept of abstraction implies that the learned policy is composed of a set of high and low-layer control policies: an upper-layer policy generates meta-actions giving instructions to a lower-layer policy. The lower-layer policy is responsible for generating the primitive actions that agents take in their environments. There are mainly four foun dational methods under hierarchical RL: options framework, MAXQ, feudal RL, and hierarchical abstract machines [32]. Hierarchical RL has outperformed primitive RL in many applications, and it has proven to be efficient and effective in solving challenging tasks such as Atari video games, management of multi-agent autonomous guided vehicles, robot soccer, etc. [33,34]. The extension of hierarchical RL applications to larger and more complex control environments is an ongoing and open research area that is receiving increasing attention. It is based on temporal abstraction in which an agent takes actions with different time scales when solving a given task. At each decision time step, the agent chooses an option (called also skill), which is suggested by an upper-layer policy (called policy-over-options) among a set of op tions. The agent then follows the lower-layer policy (called intra-option policy) that is associated with its selected option. The lower-layer policy generates the action that the agent takes in its environment. A termination function then decides whether the agent should keep the same selected option for making the next decision, or whether a new option should be selected. The option-critic approach has various advantages as compared with other hierarchical RL-based algorithms. It is an end-to-end approach that allows to automatically discover and learn the underlying temporal abstractions within a given task without the need for specifying sub-goals by hand, as is the case in other hierarchical approaches [32,35,36]. In the terminology of the options framework, three functions are learned: (1) the policy-over-options: chooses the option; (2) the intra-option policy: chooses the primitive action; and, (3) the termination function: decides whether to change the option or continue using it. ![](469995d4ff3c5bf04d53f85c2e140a6645dc654ac2ff1448a161eedf2fa40ef8.jpg) Fig. 4. Nevertheless, maintaining model accuracy, albeit at the level of each local agent, necessitates a continuous process of calibration each time a system modification is introduced. Having to do so is becoming less evident and impractical as energy systems are rapidly and constantly changing in the path towards decarbonization as DERs (especially behind-themeter ones) are increasingly put online at a rapid pace. Designing and tuning models of such stochastic and rapidly evolving networks re quires significant investments in up-front engineering resources on top of being time consuming. Although learning-based control design can take significant learning time, the process is vastly automated and does not require much engineering expertise once training algorithms are set up. Beyond algorithms, all that is required is training data, which may be readily available in the case of pre-existing installations or which may need to be synthesized based on local conditions (e.g., latitude, historic weather patterns). Another point of difference between MA-OCDDP and optimization based approaches is that MA-OCDDPG generates actions instantaneously using the networks previously learned during the of fline training phase. Nevertheless, optimization-based approaches (whether centralized or decentralized) require a process of solving an optimization problem at the beginning of each decision time step to generate optimal control decisions. The re-iteration of calculations may become problematic mainly for centralized approaches as decision time steps get shorter (in the order of seconds to minutes) or when the number of controllable units increase. Although decentralized optimization-based approaches that rely on various decomposition methods are known to be computationally efficient in comparison to centralized ones, they still require performing calculations and communicating at each decision time step. In contrast, the execution phase of MA-OCDDPG is based on generating decisions instantaneously with minimal numerical processing. The most time-consuming process of RL is its training phase where the agents need to learn how to solve a given task. A comparison of the training time of MA-OCDDPG in Experiment 2 and Experiment 3 shows that when the number of agents doubles, the training time doubles as well. Although the training time can be optimized further through specific techniques such as paralle computing or parameter sharing (only for fully cooperative problems), it does not pose a burden as the training process is performed offline and does not interfere with the real-time execution process. That is, once the training process is complete, the trained controls are put in execution in the field and fully communication-free decentralized control is possible, as each controllable unit only needs local information to make instantaneous real-time decisions. Finally, to improve the uncertainty-handling feature of optimization-based approaches, forecasts (e.g., demand, PV, wind, electricity price, etc.) are usually provided as inputs. Therefore, the control performance of these approaches usually depends on the length of their required forecasts and their accuracy. As for MA-OCDDPG, its learning feature allows it to overcome uncertainties and environment dynamic changes without requiring forecasts. It is of interest to recall that the learning feature of MA-OCDDPG allows it to adapt to changing environment dynamics and uncertainties without the need for re-training. Nevertheless, it can always benefit from continuous offline re-training based on the availability of ad ditional historical information. Likewise, continuous offline training makes the addition of new assets/agents a simple task that can be automated. ## 7. Conclusion This work proposed control approaches for energy management through scheduling the operation of controllable DERs. We have presented control strategies that can efficiently handle complex and multi objective power system control problems with uncertainties and high dimensional state and action spaces. It has been found that the im plementation of hierarchical reinforcement learning in general and the options framework in particular for solving a typical energy scheduling problem within a microgrid results in lower costs, better generaliza tion, faster convergence and enhanced stability as compared with its primitive counterpart. Furthermore, three MARL-based control strategies have been implemented for solving a multi-agent energy management problem within an eco-neighborhood, namely MADDPG, MA-A2C and MA-OCDDPG. These proposed approaches are based on CTDE, which allows to achieve coordination among different decision-making units with no communication burden nor any explicit system model. These approaches are applicable with both discrete and continuous action spaces. Experimental results have shown that MA-OCDDPG, which merges hierarchical RL with MARL theory, have resulted in the best perfor mance when compared with other control approaches, while, at the same time, comprising the merits of both sub-areas. The scalability of MA-OCDDPG has been investigated, while the solution of MA-OCDDPG has been also compared with a common model-based rolling-horizon based optimization. It has been found that MA-OCDDPG was as effec tive as the rolling-horizon approach in handling the uncertainties in generation and demand, while generating flexible and strategic control actions accordingly. Furthermore, with a higher number of controllable units, MA-OCDDPG has effectively coordinated the dispatchable units to reach desired objectives of meeting the load, reducing operation cost and maximizing self-consumption from renewable production most importantly without any real-time communication. The work presented in this paper can be extended in many directions. First, although this work has considered fully cooperative scenarios, all the proposed control approaches are also applicable to fully competitive or mixed cooperative competitive frameworks, which is a future research direction. Second, as this work provided a high-level comparison of our proposed approach with MPC considering accurate forecasts and a perfect system model to characterize upper bounds for reward values, a thorough comparison needs to be provided to evaluate the trade-offs of each approach. That is, beyond model and forecasts’ accuracy, an MPC implementation is dependent upon many elements that can strongly affect its performance such as the length of the prediction horizon, the number of uncertainty sources and their correlation, forecasts’ accuracy in relation with the prediction horizon length, real-time computational burden, etc. To establish a fair compar ison between both approaches, all these elements need to be part of the comparison framework in order to provide a thorough, balanced and realistic evaluation. Some insights to that effect are already presented in [43]. Furthermore, as this paper compared the performance of MA-OCDDPG with centralized optimization, it is of interest to compare its performance with other decentralized optimization-based approaches or distributed approaches. The trade-offs of each approach need to be thoroughly assessed. Beyond the operation cost, the comparison should cover diverse aspects, which include robustness and reliability, uncertainty handling, tractability and communication requirements. Finally, this paper adopted an extensive manual hyperparameter search based on trial-and-error to find the best possible combination of hyperparameters. Although manual hyperparameter tuning is commonly used, such practice would become more challenging, tedious and time consuming as control problems increase in complexity (e.g., when a higher number of heterogeneous decision-making units are involved) as the number of possibilities and potential control combinations would increase. This would make the search process more time-consuming, and the selection of the optimal configuration would become increas ingly difficult [44]. To overcome this difficulty, there are various options that have been proposed in the literature and have proven to be viable means for facilitating the hyperparameters selection process such as automatic hyperparameter optimization based on the integration of evolutionary algorithms [44,45]. ## CRediT authorship contribution statement Imen Jendoubi: Conceived and designed the analysis, Performed the analysis, Wrote the paper.
